newsitem.title: USA: Dollar closes higher in U.S. after Swiss sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes higher in U.S. after Swiss sell-off.

text.p: A weaker Swiss franc and dollar short-covering before Friday's key U.S. employment data helped the U.S. currency close firmer, traders said.

Mark/Swiss rose to 0.8369, its highest level in 15-months, on renewed focus on Switzerland's weak economy and concern that an investigation into wartime deposits in Switzerland might lead to the suspension of its bank secrecy laws.
But with much of Europe closed on Friday, dealers said they were keen to buy back dollars sold Wednesday before the release of U.S. jobs and manufacturing data on Friday.

"You had marks and Swiss sort of perky off and on through the course of the week," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney Inc. "You've got a European holiday, where many of the centers are closed and you have a big U.S. number.
"So, I think there was a little bit of profit-taking on that and it just gathered a bit of momentum."
The dollar rose to 1.2685/95 Swiss francs at the close from 1.2579/82 at the open and to 1.5180/90 marks from 1.5144/47.
Despite a softer mark/yen cross, dollar/yen also rose to 114.05/15 from 113.65/68 at the open.
The government releases its widely-watched report on October employment, along with September factory orders data on Friday.

Economists polled by Reuters expect non-farm payrolls to have climbed 212,000 after falling 40,000 in September. September factory orders are expected to have risen 2.3 percent after falling 1.9 percent the previous month.
The market will also look to a key index of manufacturing activity from the National Association of Purchasing Management to confirm recent signs of a U.S. economic slowdown.
Strong data would increase the possibility of a Federal Reserve interest rate increase and could spook U.S. asset and currency markets.

Dealers attributed the Swiss franc's fall in part to a wire-service report stating that Switzerland seeks to accelerate the easing of bank secrecy laws to allow experts to review the fate of Jewish money and Nazi assets deposited there in the second World War.
But Finstrom pointed out the Swiss bank secrecy laws -- long the foundation of Switzerland's investment appeal -- have been coming down for years.
Of equal importance, the Swiss franc has recently seen its historical role as a safe-haven currency erode, traders said.

"The Swiss franc market is focusing for the first time in a long time on fundamentals...because of low interest rates and because of the state of the economy," said Bill Marr, foreign exchange manager at Credit Commerciale de France. "A lot of its international appeal is not being adhered to."

The dollar closed at Canadian $1.3380/85, down from C$1.3397/02 at the open. The pound slipped to $1.6260/70 from $1.6265/75. The Australian dollar closed at $0.7912/17 down from $0.7916/21. -- Alden Bentley 212 859 1667
